newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metal union leader affirms strike readiness.
newsitem.headline: German metal union leader affirms strike readiness.

text.p: Klaus Zwickel, chairman of the IG Metall trade union, on Tuesday confirmed Germany's largest trade union would be ready to strike from early next year following the collapse of talks to solve a bitter sick pay row.
Zwickel said the breakdown on Tuesday morning of talks between regional negotiators in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia represented the last chance to solve the dispute "amicably".
Any further negotiations would now take place "following the cancellation of wage contracts and outside the necessary strike notice period," Zwickel said in a statement.
Referring to the possibility of strikes after the four-week notice period required by German law, he added "If no peaceable settlement is reached, we shall also do that."

Officials at IG Metall, which has nearly three million members nationwide, had earlier said strikes could go ahead as early as next March if no agreement is reached on the issue during the 1997 wage round scheduled for the start of next year.
The dispute on sick pay was triggered by a new law in October allowing employers to cut payments from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.

The talks in North Rhine- Westphalia, a key steel-making region, were the latest in a series of failed attempts to produce a regional deal that could then have been proposed as a "pilot agreement" on a national level.
Overall, metal and engineering employers are seeking a 1997 wage deal that would leave overall labour costs in the sector unchanged.
Union leaders are meanwhile aiming to secure agreements protecting jobs in the sector.
